Pattern

Card

Hover a card. The whole card is the target, not the title — the shadow lifts, the image zooms 6%, and the product itself glows. That last one works because filter: drop-shadow reads the alpha channel and traces the actual silhouette rather than the box, so a cut-out PNG glows around the product. It only works on a cut-out: an image with an opaque background gets a rectangular glow and looks broken, which makes the transparent-PNG column in the licence register a rendering requirement now. The title no longer underlines. Price sits to the right of the title; on a discount the old price stays on the right and the new one drops below it.

Pattern

Button

Three and no more. The amber one carries .d-finish for the plywood surface, but .d-btn alone still renders a solid amber button — a pattern that goes transparent when someone forgets a second class will eventually ship transparent. Two amber buttons side by side means neither is the answer, so the second choice is outlined.

Pattern

Band

Full bleed is the default, not a modifier — the colour runs edge to edge and the content takes the gutter. Built on a grid rather than negative margins, because a negative margin has to cancel whatever padding its wrapper happens to have, and when it over-cancels you get a horizontal scrollbar at exactly one viewport width that nobody tests for.

Pattern

Notice

A notice is a tinted surface with a solid edge, never a solid block — a full-bleed red panel across a checkout reads as a crash rather than as a correction, and the checkout is where a customer is most likely to abandon. Every state carries an icon as well as a tint: roughly one man in twelve cannot separate the red one from the green one, and a tint this light does almost nothing on a bad screen in daylight. The icon is a pseudo-element, because WooCommerce emits these and we cannot add an <svg> to its markup.

The stars are drawn with clip-path, not typed. U+2726 is missing from plenty of system fonts and falls back to a tofu box, and an error message is the worst place to find that out.

Every animation here is off on the money path. motion.css kills animation on cart, checkout and order-received, and under reduced motion — and notices appear on those pages more than anywhere else. So the resting frame is the real design and the motion is a bonus. Each state is composed to read at frame zero with its stars already in position, rather than starting stacked in the middle.

The stars own the whole element now. Error rains them from above across the full width; warning walks one around the text on an ellipse; success has five darting about; info points from above and from the far side. They sit behind the text at z-index 0 — a star crossing a word is a legibility bug dressed up as whimsy — and overflow:hidden keeps them inside the box.

Eleven stars, no JavaScript. The notice's two pseudo-elements plus three empty spans of three each. That is what “continuously” costs without a script.

Erratic is a timing problem, not a path problem. The excited ones run on linear timing with keyframe stops at uneven intervals — 13, 24, 41, 55, 69, 88. An ease makes every leg accelerate and settle the same way, which reads as a route being followed however wild the path is; uneven stops read as a mind being changed.

The orbit and the pokes aim at the text now, anchored in em over the left third rather than centred on the box.

The close is a plain X now. It was a star, then a spinning star, and that was the loudest gesture on the page attached to the least important thing anyone will do on it. Cocoa to claret, nothing else.

Pattern

Rating

One star shape, masked and repeated — not five elements. A rating is 4.3 as often as it is 4, so the fill has to be able to stop part way through a star. Five separate elements can’t do that without a sixth overlay each. Instead the whole strip is a two-stop gradient — gold up to the value, ash after it — and a mask punches five stars out of it. A half star costs nothing, and it is the same eight-point star as the notices use.

In a row, with the count

4,3 · 27 отзива

The interactive one. Hover it, and tab into it. Underneath is a real radio group — a rating is an input, so it has to be reachable by keyboard and announced properly. The stars are the visible layer and the radios sit on top at zero opacity, so a click or a tap lands on the control rather than on a decoration. The fill follows :has(), so there is no script. Hover the fourth star — the first four lift and shine together. That is :has() reading forwards, which used to need reversed DOM order and a ~ combinator.

This one is five real elements; the read-only one above is not. A mask over a single gradient can stop part way through a star, which the read-only version needs and an input never does — you cannot leave 3.4 stars. But one element cannot transform part of itself, so the lift forced the interactive version onto discrete elements. Same shape, two constructions, on purpose.

WooCommerce’s rating is a font glyph, and it has to be silenced. .star-rating renders black stars as ::before text content in a font we don’t load; left alone they show through our mask as black stars behind gold ones. font-size:0 stops it — display:none would collapse the width Woo uses to express the value, which is the same width we then paint gold to get a partial fill for free.

Open: empty stars are --c-ash-300, the warm grey. Against the new grey-050 card they may want to be cooler. Say if they look muddy to you.

Pattern

Field

Every control, and every state. Three rules run through all of them. The message always has room — the error is not inserted on failure, its space is reserved from the start, because a checkout that grows by 18px per invalid field pushes the button out from under a thumb that was already moving toward it. The state is never colour alone — an invalid field gets a thicker edge, a star and a sentence. And focus is a ring plus a colour, never the browser outline removed with nothing put back.

Pattern

Table

The row is carried by tone, the column by a rule. This reverses what I built first — I had horizontal hairlines and no vertical rules, which left the table doing nothing to help the eye stay on a row and wasted the one separator that survives the collapse to a phone. Now: alternating row tone does the row, a vertical rule does the column, and there are no horizontal rules at all except above a total. Numbers are tabular and right-aligned, because a column of prices whose decimal points do not line up is unreadable at a glance, and the glance is the entire point of a totals column.

Two collapse mechanisms, and the markup forced both. Below 600px a table stops being a table — horizontal scrolling inside a cart is how an order gets abandoned. The classic WooCommerce tables carry data-title on every cell, so each value can label itself with content:attr(data-title); the first table uses that, narrow your window to see it — and note that the stripe is what keeps one stacked record distinct from the next, since at that width a horizontal hairline between rows would be indistinguishable from one between cells. The block cart carries no such attribute — captured and checked — so its three columns re-lay with grid instead: image on the left spanning two lines, product and total stacked beside it. Writing one mechanism and hoping it covered both is how a cart ends up unreadable at 390px.

Patterns

Quantity, badge

Quantity. The input stays a real number field — somebody typing 12 must not press + eleven times — and the buttons are a convenience either side of it. They are 2.6em, about 44px: these are the smallest things anyone taps in the whole purchase, Woo’s own are around 28px, and a miss here changes a quantity you did not mean to change.

Badge. Never clickable and never looks it — no shadow, no lift, no pointer. Over a photograph it takes the scrim, the one non-text use of cocoa in the system, because a tint alone disappears on a light image.

Ново -30% Само 2 броя Изборът на Lady D Намаление
Captured, not assumed: in Woo’s quantity selector the buttons come after the input in source order, so the minus is not the first child. The adopted rules use grid areas rather than flex order, which keeps the tab sequence matching the visual one — reordering with order would have left a keyboard user tabbing minus, plus, then the field.

Pattern

Panel

A heading you can press. Where we own the markup it is <details>/<summary> — a real disclosure widget with no script — because the clearest case is the coupon panel on the checkout, and somebody arriving with a discount code who cannot reach the field by keyboard simply does not complete the order. Measured on the live site with a seeded cart: /cart/ renders one .wc-block-components-panel and /checkout/ renders one, and both are the coupon.

The swimmer. Open one. The arrow rides the opening edge down the panel, reaches the bottom and turns a full half-circle — a tumble turn, not a mirror flip — and leaves a streak that is brightest halfway across and gone at both ends. Close it and the whole thing runs backwards.

It is not an animation. An animation keyed to [open] plays once and cannot play backwards when the attribute is removed, so a closing panel would snap. Everything here is arithmetic on one registered custom property, --swim, transitioned 0 → 1: the arrow’s top is head + swim × (100% − 2×head) where the 100% is the panel’s own animating height, and the trail’s opacity is 1 − 2×abs(swim − .5), which peaks mid-stroke and is zero at rest. Backwards comes free.

Two honest limits. 1. abs() is Chrome 133+. Every declaration that uses it is written twice, safe value first, so an older browser drops the trail and keeps the swim and the turn. Decoration must fail to nothing. 2. On Woo’s own panel the “rides the opening edge” part cannot work: it is a div plus a button whose content React mounts and unmounts, so there is no height to interpolate and no ::details-content to hook. The content appears at once and the arrow swims down through it. The turn and the trail still work.

Patterns

Pagination, skeleton

Pagination. Click through the numbers and watch what moves. In the middle of the run the numbers shift and the circle stays put; at either end the numbers cannot shift any further, so the circle moves instead. That is not two rules with an if between them — it is one clamp():

offset = clamp(0, page − 1 − half, pages − window), and the marker sits at (page − 1 − offset) × cell. In the middle offset tracks page one-for-one so the marker is constant; at the ends the clamp pins offset so the marker does the moving. One line, both behaviours, and they cannot disagree with each other.

The wake is two clocks. A trail has to know where the thing came from, and CSS has no memory of a previous value. So the position is transitioned twice at different speeds — --pg-a at 360ms is the marker, --pg-b at 620ms is a ghost of it. The wake spans between them: zero width at rest, widest mid-move, and it points backwards on its own, because the ghost is simply late.

Every target is 2.75em, about 44px. These sit at the bottom of a long scroll, are used most on a phone, and are the last thing between somebody and the rest of the catalogue.

The limit, and it is the important one. WooCommerce pagination is a set of links. Clicking one is a document navigation, and a CSS transition cannot cross a page load — the old document is gone before the new one paints. Making this animate on the real shop needs cross-document view transitions (@view-transition{ navigation: auto }, Chrome 126+), which changes the feel of every navigation on the site and not just the paginator. That is your call, so it is written down and not switched on. Everything above works today inside one document, which is what you are clicking.

Skeleton. The shape of content that has not arrived — and it has to read with the animation switched off. motion.css kills every animation on cart, checkout and order-received and under reduced motion, which are precisely the pages that show skeletons; a skeleton built as nothing but a moving highlight is invisible on the one page it exists for. So the resting tone is the design and the shimmer is a bonus. The shimmer is a transform on a pseudo-element rather than an animated background position, because a grid of twenty skeletons is the worst possible place to repaint every frame — the page is already busy fetching the thing they stand in for.

The same three with the shimmer killed, as they appear on the checkout — still legible as placeholders

Patterns

Slider, scrollbar

I probed the browser before writing either of these, in the same Chrome you are running (141). The customisable range spec — appearance:base on input[type=range], ::slider-fill, ::slider-track — is not shipped yet. Firefox paints the filled part itself via ::-moz-range-progress; Chrome has no way to, because CSS cannot read an input’s value.

So the slider works completely with no script — track, thumb, keyboard, focus ring, all three colours — and one small script file — assets/darling-ui.js — adds the fill and the wake by mirroring the value into --val. Without it --val stays 0: the fill reads empty and the wake never appears. Degraded, never broken. That file is the only script the whole design system has, and everything in it is something CSS provably cannot do. I am not going to claim a pure-CSS fill in Chrome, because there is not one.

The wake used to be in the wrong place, and the reason is worth knowing. It was positioned with transform: translate(...), and the expression contained a percentage — but in a transform, percentages resolve against the element’s own box, not the container. The wake’s own width is the length of the gap, so where the streak sat depended on how far the thumb had just moved: near the left on a slow drag, creeping right on a fast one. Percentages in left resolve against the containing block, so that is what places it now.

The wake is better here than on the paginator. --val is set raw on every input event so the thumb never lags your pointer; --sl-a is a transitioned copy that chases it. Drag fast and the streak is long; nudge it with an arrow key and it is short. That is a real velocity, not a faked one — try both.

grey — default

cherry — golden wake

gold — cherry wake

Scrollbars, and the honest part. First, a measurement: on the live site with a seeded cart, nothing on /cart/ or /checkout/ actually scrolls — I counted every element whose computed overflow is auto or scroll and whose content overflows, and it is zero on both. So a scroll region is not a money-path surface today.

A native scrollbar cannot carry a trail. scrollbar-color takes two colours and nothing else; ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb is a real box but has no way to know it is moving and cannot own a pseudo-element behind it. There is no arrangement of CSS that puts a wake behind a native thumb. A trailing scrollbar means replacing the scrollbar — which is the second row below.

Native, branded — two colours, no markup, works everywhere

What our own scrollbar actually costs. It knows exactly where you are — a scroll timeline is continuous and exact, and the thumb tracks the position to the pixel with no script at all. Nothing about “where we are” is missing. What it does not get free is what the operating system gives a native bar: dragging (a native thumb is draggable because the OS draws it; ours is a div — nine lines of script), its own length (the thumb should be viewport÷content long, and CSS cannot see scrollHeight), a clock (a scroll timeline is a position: it says “you are 42% down” perfectly, but it has no memory, so there is no “where was I 200ms ago” and therefore no velocity and therefore no trail), and OS integration (assistive tech, high-contrast, the “always show scrollbars” setting, re-measuring when content changes). All four are covered by assets/darling-ui.js — so these three are draggable, and they do trail. The trade is that we now own that behaviour instead of the OS.
One thing the probe turned up that changes an answer I gave you. ::scroll-button(), ::scroll-marker and scroll-driven animations are all live in your Chrome. That means a carousel with real prev/next buttons and dot indicators is now possible with no JavaScript at all — which is a much better answer to your carousel question than “WooCommerce doesn’t ship one”. Say the word and that is the next component.

Pattern

Icons

This one is not decoration — it is what stage 4 of the dequeue is blocked on. woocommerce.css declares two @font-face families and paints 12 distinct private-use glyphs from them across 19 rules. The font loads on every page type and 5 glyphs render on the product page. Take that stylesheet away before we own the marks and the product page shows empty boxes.

Masks, not a font, and not inline SVG. A font makes every icon a character: it inherits letter-spacing, it can be selected and copied into an order note, it falls back to a box when the font fails. Inline SVG puts the mark in the markup, so one mark used in forty places is forty copies. A mask over background: currentColor is neither — the mark is the ink, so it takes the colour of whatever it sits in, on hover, inside a cherry button, in Windows High Contrast, with no extra rules.

It takes the ink of whatever it is in

  В количката
The glyph table, so the next person can check the work rather than trust it: \e00a downloads → download, \e013 remove-a-filter → close, \e015 message → check, \e016 error → error, \e017 added-to-cart → check, \e019 shipping-calculator → chevron, \e01c loading → spinner, \e028 info → info, \e02d email → mail, \e037 phone → phone. The two star glyphs are deliberately absent: the rating pattern already draws stars with clip-path, font-independently, and pointing them at a mask would be a second implementation of a solved thing.

Windows High Contrast strips background images, and this mark is a background — so without a forced-colors rule every icon would vanish silently, still 1em, still taking space, painting nothing. There is one.

Patterns

Header, nav, mega menu, search

Ported from style.css, and the port is not a copy. --d-honey-light became --tint-gold, so a hovered nav link and a hovered panel row are now the same colour by token rather than by coincidence. The search pill was the last hard #fff left on the page. Three hand-typed radii for the same job became --radius-s. The inline SVGs became .d-icon.

Two behaviour changes, both deliberate. The mega menu opened on :hover and :focus-within only — unreachable on a touch screen that does not emulate hover. Both are kept, and a real <button aria-expanded> is added alongside. And the current page is now underlined as well as coloured, because colour alone is the one cue a colour-blind visitor does not get.

Drawers

Both are real <dialog> elements, which the old markup already got right and is worth keeping for reasons easy to lose in a rewrite: a dialog traps focus, returns it to whatever opened it, closes on Escape, makes the page behind it inert, and gets ::backdrop free. A <div class="drawer"> gets none of that.

The open animation changed from a keyframe to @starting-style. The old rule was animation: darling-drawer-in .22s on [open] — which plays once on open and cannot play backwards, so the drawer slid in and then simply vanished. Same lesson as the panel's swim: transitions reverse, animations do not.

Към плащане

Icon motion, and the progress bar

Your rule, and it is the right one: a mark moves only when something happens. Nothing idles. An interface where six small things are all moving is not lively, it is noisy — and the one mark that is reporting something gets lost in the other five.

A mask is one silhouette, so it cannot have a spinning wheel in it. The marks that move are split: the still part is the element's own mask, and each moving part is a pseudo-element with its own mask and its own transform-origin. Two pseudo-elements is the budget — which is exactly two wheels, or one bow — and that limit is why the trail on an added-to-cart lives on the button rather than on the icon.

always press me hover hover tick me hover hover hover hover
Deliberately still: mail, phone, info, warning, error, the stars inside a rating, plus and minus. The notices those sit on already animate — falling stars, an orbiting star, the excited ones — and two animations on one object compete. The heart is a real <input type="checkbox">, so :checked does the work: no script, keyboard-reachable, and a screen reader says “checked” without an aria attribute anyone has to remember.

Progress — three variants, and the sheen is clipped to the filled part

A shine that travels over the empty part says the empty part is doing something, which is the opposite of what the bar is for — so the sheen lives inside the fill and is clipped to it by construction. When the bar completes it turns gold and runs three times, then stops: a bar that keeps celebrating at somebody trying to pay is a distraction, not a reward.

One real limitation. The native <progress> is the accessible default and it is styled to match — but it cannot have the sheen, because ::-webkit-progress-value cannot own a pseudo-element. That is why the div version exists at all, and it carries role="progressbar" with the numbers on it.

The clear button sweeps the field and takes the text with it — type in the header search and press the x

One clock drives both. --wipe goes 1→0; the x sits at calc(--wipe × travel) and the input is masked with a hard-edged gradient whose stop is at the same place, so the text cannot survive the sweep or vanish ahead of it. The streak is the two-clock trail again — --wipe-b lags, and the wake spans between them.

Being straight about “letter by letter”: the mask edge moves continuously. It crosses one glyph at a time so letters do go out one after another, but a letter is clipped mid-stroke as the edge passes rather than disappearing whole. Snapping per character means wrapping every character in its own element and rebuilding that on each keystroke. Say the word if you want it; I do not think it is worth the cost.

Patterns

Category banner, grid, archive, carousel

Twenty-eight rules of content were living in the stylesheet. style.css carried one image-set rule per category, then again inside a 700px query, hard-coding ten term slugs and thirty file paths. Adding a category meant editing CSS; renaming a term silently lost its banner; and nobody could tell by reading the file which images actually exist on disk. Two of those are invisible until a customer lands on the page.

The folder is the source of truth now — scripts/gen-category-banners.js reads assets/img/banners/ and writes src/generated/category-banners.css. 11 banners found, 11 rules, 9 narrow overrides; the hand-written version had 28, half of them a 700px query that repeated the 1x source as the 2x source. A term with no image is now reported at build time instead of rendering an empty claret box.

Carousel — a real scroller, with the buttons your carousel.js already drives

За кухнятаЗа банятаЗа децатаЗа градинатаПодаръциПромоцииПартиПочистване
The row is a scroller, not a transform — it already was, and that was the right call: a real overflow container can be swiped, flicked, trackpad-dragged, tabbed through and navigated by a screen reader. A translated strip does none of those and has to reimplement every one in script. Only the two arrows need carousel.js.

The scriptless version is parked, and I would rather say why than leave a tempting comment. ::scroll-button() and ::scroll-marker would give this row prev/next controls and dot indicators with no JavaScript at all, and both report as supported in your Chrome. But ::scroll-marker crashes the renderer with this stylesheet — “Target crashed” before first paint, bisected on the real page, and five hand-written minimal reproductions did not reproduce it, so I know what to remove and not yet why. And ::scroll-button() rendered but would not place: anchor(top) + 50% is not the anchor’s middle, and anchor(center), which is, computed to top: auto and dropped the button in the bottom-left corner. Two failures and a browser crash on one feature is where to stop.

Patterns

Tabs

One row of labels, one panel showing at a time, and an underline that travels. The mark is not a background on the selected tab — a background cannot move between two elements, and moving is the whole point. It is two bars on one pair of values, --tab-x and --tab-w, transitioned on two different clocks: the cherry mark on the UI curve arrives first, the gold ghost on the wake curve is still catching up, and the lit gap between them is the trail. Nothing computes a direction; the sign of the gap falls out of the ghost being late. Same trick as the panel’s swimmer and the paginator’s wake.

Tab widths depend on their text, so unlike the paginator there is no cell size to multiply an index by, and CSS cannot measure a box. darling-ui.js measures the selected tab and publishes the two numbers. Until it has, the CSS draws no travelling bar at all and the selected tab carries a plain static underline — so a page whose script failed to load still has a correct tab strip, just a still one. The two are never both drawn.

Patterns

Product page — gallery, buy column, trust, tabs, reviews

This is the most contested page on the site. collide.js counts 209 element/property pairs here where our CSS and WooCommerce’s both have an opinion — more than home, shop and checkout put together. Everything below is wrapped in .woocommerce > div.product and uses Woo’s class names, because a fixture written with our own classes would render perfectly and prove nothing about who wins.

Two defects that are live on darlinghome.bg right now, measured this morning. WooCommerce builds each tab’s shape out of two 5×5px pseudo-elements per tab — quarter-round corners with a lilac border and a lilac box-shadow. style.css zeroes the tab’s own background and border but never touched its pseudos, so all four nubs are still painting: 2 of 2 tabs, border rgb(207,200,216), shadow rgb(233,230,237). And style.css tries to kill Woo’s full-width underline with content:none at specificity (0,3,1) against Woo’s (0,3,2) — it loses, so Woo’s lilac rule and ours are both drawn, one over the other. The same arithmetic ate the strip’s padding: ours says 0, Woo says 1em, computed is 17px.

What is measured here and what is not. The tab rules were verified against the live product page. The gallery and the review list were not: the shop has exactly one product, it has no images and no reviews, so there is no live DOM for either. They are written against WooCommerce’s own stylesheet and its review.php markup and rendered against this fixture. Re-check them the day a photographed product with a review exists.

Напиши отзив

12345

The stars come out on the click and only on the click. They were doing both — out on hover, then thrown again on the click — because burst.css’s hover rules were written as a bare :hover back when hover was the only trigger. They are scoped away from click hosts now, so the season banner keeps its hover and the buy button has one event. Four times the size, nine of them, 1.5s, and twice as far as the first attempt threw them.

The review form was not styled badly — it was not styled at all. Everything in adopted/field.css targets either the block checkout or the classic checkout, and WooCommerce’s review form is neither: it is WordPress’s comment form, a bare <textarea id="comment"> with no .input-text and no .form-row. Not one rule was selecting it.

The rating picker had the shape but not the behaviour. Woo emits <p class="stars"><span> and my fixture said <span class="stars">, so p.stars never matched and five bare links rendered as the text “1 2 3 4 5”. Now they lift and a band of light sweeps across them, the same as .d-rating-input — in two selectors rather than fifteen, by asking “does a hovered star come after me?” instead of enumerating every combination. Still not right: these are anchors. Woo’s picker needs JavaScript, cannot be operated from the keyboard and tells a screen reader nothing. .d-rating-input is five real radios and has none of those problems; swapping them is a PHP change to woocommerce_comment_form_rating().

The travelling underline is not a background on the active tab. A background cannot move between two elements, and moving is the whole point. It is two bars on one pair of values — --tab-x and --tab-w — transitioned on two different clocks: the cherry mark on the UI curve arrives first, the gold ghost on the wake curve is still catching up, and the lit gap between them is the trail. It points backwards without anything computing a direction, because the ghost is simply late. Same trick as the panel’s swimmer and the paginator’s wake.

They are Woo’s own pseudo-elements, taken over rather than added. ul.tabs::before is Woo’s lilac rule and ::after is a clearfix; both are redefined, which kills the lilac and costs no extra markup. Hanging them on the first li instead does not work — a pseudo-element is positioned against its own element, so it would measure --tab-x from that tab’s left edge rather than the strip’s.

With no script there is no bar at all. Tab widths depend on their text, so something has to measure; darling-ui.js adds .d-tabs-live once it has, and until then the selected tab carries a plain static underline. The two are never both drawn.

The thumbnails are a grid and none of them are dimmed. Woo floats them at 25% and then needs clear:left on every 4n+1 child, once per column count; and it fades every inactive thumb to opacity:.5, which on a warm-grey page reads as “still loading”. Ours are all at full strength with a gold ring on the active one — a mark that says “this one” rather than dimming everything that is not.

The footer idles, and that is the one deliberate exception. Everywhere else in this system a mark moves only when something happens. The bow is the brand mark at the very bottom of the page, and a slow rise and fall reads as the page breathing rather than as something asking for attention — the same call you already made on the hero. Three stars twinkle with it, staggered, so they are never all bright at once. motion.css still kills every one of them on cart, checkout and order-received.

The wordmark is plain ink, and that is your ruling, not a shortcut. “We shouldn’t use the texture on text — it makes it hard to read.” finish.css records the deleted .d-finish--text with do not reintroduce this beside it, and I reintroduced it anyway by reading the legacy .darling-wordmark mapping without noticing that what it maps to is a comment rather than a rule. The check caught it.

The two stars on the newsletter band are masks, not dingbats. The legacy pair were content set to a dingbat character, which made them text: selectable, copied with the page, and read out by a screen reader as “black four pointed star”.

The email field cannot be the field pattern. .d-field draws a light surface with a grey edge, which on claret is a hole. This one is the band’s own colour a shade deeper with a lit edge — and its focus ring is cream rather than --focus-ring, because a cocoa ring on claret is invisible. That is the only place in the system where the focus token is deliberately not used.

The social circles lost three of their four hover properties. Legacy moved them, recoloured them, changed the background and grew a coloured box-shadow, all on a 42px circle.

Patterns

Accessibility mode, prose, blog, 404, consent, GPSR

The accessibility switch existed and the mode did not. Three html.d-a11y rules were already scattered across the hero, the season band and the category banner, each forcing a title to white on a dark photograph. That was all of it: no text size, no underlines, no animation kill, no focus change. The switch was in the markup and in the legacy stylesheet, and in our system it did three things to three headings.

And the type scale cannot be scaled from the root. The legacy mode did html.darling-a11y body{ font-size:17px }, which works because those sizes were relative. Ours are not — tokens/type.css declares --fs-body:16px and the rest in pixels, so a root font-size change moves nothing at all. The mode redeclares nine size tokens instead, which is the mechanism a token system is for. The better fix some day is one multiplier, and then those nine lines become one.

Two of these are not new components. The GPSR block is a disclosure and a warning, and we already have .d-panel and .d-notice. The legacy stylesheet wrote a third disclosure and a fourth notice for it. Both are gone.

Consent card and the two buttons — shown here in place rather than fixed to the window

Използваме бисквитки, за да работи количката и да разберем кое си струва. Повече

EN
The two buttons are bottom-LEFT, and that is not arbitrary. Bottom-right is where every chat widget, cookie nag and back-to-top button goes, and this is the control somebody needs when all of those are in the way.

The consent card clears them by variable, not by 78px. The legacy version hard-coded the gap, which is correct until somebody changes a button’s size — and then it is a card sitting on top of the accessibility switch, the one control a person in that situation most needs to reach.

The mode is the only place !important is allowed. Everywhere else in this system an !important is a specificity argument somebody lost. Here it is the point: a person who asked for the plain version gets it whatever any component says, including components written after this file.

Quiet ink becomes ordinary ink in the mode, which flattens the hierarchy on purpose — it trades “you can see what is secondary” for “you can read everything”, which is the trade somebody makes by turning it on. Worth a look with the switch flipped before it ships.

Patterns

Checkout add-ons — VAT invoice and the office picker

This one is mostly a deletion. The two blocks carried 28 legacy rules and all but a handful were the system saying something twice: field borders and radii, a focus ring (amber — every other field in the system is cocoa), an invalid state, a hint, an error, a warning notice and a radio. They are .d-field__control, .d-field--invalid, .d-field__hint, .d-field__error, .d-notice--warning and .d-check. What is left is a card, a grid and a disabled state.

Nothing here animates, deliberately. motion.css kills every animation and transition on body.woocommerce-checkout, and these two blocks live nowhere else — so a transition written here is dead code that looks alive.

And what the order review prints

Еконт · София, ул. Пример 12

Офисът не е потвърден от куриера. Ще се свържем с вас преди изпращане.

The unconfirmed warning is a hard-coded colour in PHP. class-office-field.php prints <span style="color:#b01f30"> straight into the order review. It is one shade off --notice-error-edge, it is not in any stylesheet, and the cutover will therefore not find it — deleting style.css changes nothing about it. It wants to be a .d-notice--warning, and that is a plugin change rather than a theme one.

The select is the system's select. .d-field select already draws our chevron, so the picker needs no rule of its own; the four states above are markup and copy, not CSS. The one thing they do need is the disabled state, which is why the loading select is really disabled rather than merely grey.

The submit, blocked

The layout spans by class, not by id. Legacy said .di-fields #di-company, .di-fields #di-address{ grid-column:1/-1 } — the layout keyed to two specific fields by name, so a third long field means editing CSS and renaming one silently drops it back into half a column.

The courier block is a stack, not a grid. City and office are dependent — you cannot pick an office before a city — and putting a dependent pair side by side invites filling the second one first.

The blocked button keeps its focus. A disabled button cannot be focused, so a keyboard user tabbing to the end of the checkout finds nothing and no explanation of why. The style is on aria-disabled as well, so the plugin can leave the button enabled and put the reason in the field error — which is where somebody is actually looking.

Greyscale as well as opacity. A cherry button at 50% is still cherry and still reads as the live action; on the plywood button opacity alone barely registers.

Pattern

Failed image

This is an error state, not a placeholder. The panel refuses to flag a product sellable online without an image, so a card with no picture means something upstream is wrong — a placeholder that escaped the rule, or a src that 404s. A pretty grey box would hide that, so the slab writes a sentence instead. It is built by assets/img-fallback.js, because CSS can neither see a broken <img> nor write a sentence; the stylesheet only decides how it looks.

The three below are one component at three widths. The caption disappears under 120px through a container query — what matters is the size of the slab, not of the window — which is why the cart drawer's 64px thumbnail needs no rule of its own. The bow is aria-hidden and the accessible name sits on the container, so nothing is lost when it goes.

And the three other things batch nine shipped

All four went into the stylesheet; only the slab went onto the page. A component that is only in the stylesheet does not exist, so here are the other three.

1. .d-section-title — the heading that names a band. Legacy declared it four separate times across four slices, each adding a font-size or a margin to the last, and all four said the same size. What is worth looking at is not the title, it is the gap ABOVE and BELOW it: an eyebrow labels the heading beneath it, so proximity has to bind downward. On the live home page three of them had 0px above and 42px below, which reads as a caption hanging off the bottom of the previous section.

Pattern

Office and locker picker

The map is an enhancement over the list, never a replacement. The list is what works with no JavaScript, on a slow connection and in a screen reader — and it is what still works when the tile host is down. A map that replaces it takes all three away for a picture. So the real <select> stays underneath, the list is the control, and the map reflects it and can drive it: either way round, neither one required.

Tiles: OpenFreeMap. Renderer: MapLibre GL. Surveyed today — no API key, no registration, no cookies, no request limit, commercial use explicit, and the whole production stack is open-source so we can host it ourselves when we want to. What it has not got is an SLA, which is exactly why the paragraph above is a rule rather than a nicety. Stadia’s free tier is non-commercial, CARTO’s Positron wants an enterprise licence, and openstreetmap.org’s own tiles forbid this use outright.

We do not need a geocoder. Speedy and Econt return their offices with their own coordinates — that is what office-picker.js already fetches. The map is a backdrop and pins we place, so the only thing that has to be good in Bulgaria is street rendering, which is ordinary OpenStreetMap. That is most of my “patchy coverage” worry answered: it was aimed at a layer we are not using.

Nothing here loads anything. The frame is a sized, styled hole for MapLibre to mount into, filled by the pattern’s own hatching. A review document that quietly pings a third party every time it is opened has opinions about privacy nobody agreed to.

The pin is our mark, not the library’s. A teardrop with the four-point star punched out of it, so the marker on the map and the bullet in the list are the same shape. Selected is bigger and gold: colour alone is the one cue a colour-blind visitor does not get, and this is the cue that says where the order is going.

Attribution is a licence condition, not a credit. It is in the pattern, so removing it means deleting a rule with a comment above it saying that.

Still to decide before the map itself is built: whether we ship MapLibre’s ~200 KB on the checkout for every visitor or load it only when the office option is chosen (the second, almost certainly), and whether the pins cluster — Sofia has over two hundred offices and Speedy returns them all.

Adopted

Catalogue filters

It is a trigger and a dialog, not a sidebar. Read off the live archive rather than assumed — which matters, because most of this batch turns out to be composition: the trigger is .d-btn--quiet and the panel is .d-drawer, and we own both. The markup below is WooCommerce’s, class for class, down to the data-wp-on--click attributes.

The open state is .is-overlay-opened on the block root, set at runtime by the Interactivity API and therefore nowhere in the served HTML. I know it because I read blocks/woocommerce/product-filters-style.css — a 5 KB per-block sheet WordPress inlines rather than links, which is why it never appeared in any stylesheet list we have taken and why the first surface inventory did not know it existed. Here it is added by hand, because a static page has no runtime.

Two modes, one markup. A dialog under 900px and a sidebar above it — the archive already has a sticky 250px column and the filters belong in it. Same breakpoint as the header’s, so the page changes shape once rather than twice. Both are below.

The sheet, at the width it is actually used at. Two things are true and I overstated them last time: a position: fixed element cannot be contained by a box, and a viewport media query cannot be faked by one. Neither stops this page from overriding those two things for itself. Inside the frame below, fixed is turned into absolute and the desktop mode is switched back off. That is the entire fake. The surface, the corner, the shadow, the header, the scrolling body, the hairline footer and the apply button are the shipped stylesheet, unmodified. The overriding rules live in this document’s own <style>, not in the theme — a rule whose only reader is a review document is a second component wearing a disguise.

And it is not a centred modal. It is a sheet from the left edge, full height, the same shape and the same arrival as our cart drawer — which is deliberate: it is the same gesture, so it should be the same object. The greyed-out ground is the scrim, and it now closes on a click, like the drawers.

Everything below the shell is a floor, not a finish, and it is marked as one in the stylesheet. The price filter renders EMPTY on the live archive — one product in the catalogue, so there is no range — and the attribute, stock, rating and chip blocks are not in the template at all. Their rules are written against WooCommerce’s stylesheet rather than against captured markup, which is exactly the method that made field.css wrong twice: Woo puts the label AFTER the input and floats it, and no amount of reading the stylesheet tells you that. Re-verify against the real DOM the day the catalogue lands.

The price pair wants to become .d-slider--pair. We already own the two-handle slider; what is here is two number inputs wearing our field, because there is no live range to build the slider against yet.

select.orderby was the last bare select on the catalogue. It has no .d-field around it, so the field pattern’s selector list never reached it and it has been rendering as the browser’s own control this whole time.

Rules

Layout primitives — the small closed set everything is composed from

A page is not a list of components. It is components inside layouts, and there are only a handful of layouts in any website. Naming them is what stops each surface inventing its own spacing: eight primitives, and every arrangement on the site is a composition of them.

The rule they exist to make possible: a surface owns padding, a layout owns gaps, and a component owns neither. That is why a checkbox can go inside a panel inside a table without anyone having to reason about it — the checkbox has no opinion about what is above it, so it cannot be wrong about it. Nesting goes wrong through double padding, not through alignment.

Eight primitives now: shell, split, stack, grid, cluster, box, switcher, frame. Four of them are new and nothing has been converted to them yet — the hand-written flex rows in the header, footer, filters, card actions and payment icons are still hand-written. Converting them is worth doing after the composition matrix, not before, because the matrix is what will say which of those hand-written rows were actually wrong.

And one rule is stated but not yet enforced: a component never sets its own outer margin. Known offenders are listed at the foot of src/patterns/layout.css — .d-intake, .d-courier, and two adopted WooCommerce families. The matrix gate is what will hold the line, by measuring the rendered margin rather than grepping for the word.

Rules

Alignment — what lines up with what, and with the page

Most of what reads as untidy on a real page is not a component being wrong. It is two correct components starting in slightly different places, and neither one’s own screenshot can show it.

Measured at 1440, with only the built stylesheet loaded: the page had three left rails. x=180 for the header and its logo, x=220 for every section title, grid, archive, product and hero, and the mega menu’s columns at the page maximum’s own edge with no gutter at all. Nobody chose that: seven files each wrote max-width:var(--page-max) beside their own padding, and two reached for --space-s where the other five used --gutter. A rule repeated in seven files is seven chances to differ, and the difference is invisible in every one of them.

The frame is now one class — .d-shell in src/patterns/layout.css — and every guide below is positioned with the same token the component reads. The line is not an opinion about where the rail is; it is the rail, so a component that misses it is missing its own token.

The vertical axis is alignment too, and the first version of this section only drew one of the two. With the guides on, the gold behind the field grid is its --space-xs gap and the pink strips are the .d-field__error lines. That is the answer to “why is there so much padding under a field”: there is none. Every field keeps a line in reserve for its error message, always, so a form cannot grow by 18 px per invalid field under a thumb that is already moving toward the button. It is the one piece of empty space on the page that is doing a job.

The aside is 21rem, not a percentage. A percentage column keeps shrinking until the summary’s own two-column rows wrap, at window sizes nobody opens on a desktop to check. Below 62rem it stops being a column and becomes the next block down — narrow this page to see it. The stand-in surface inside it is exactly that: a box drawn from tokens, not a component we have agreed on.

3 · THE CONTROL COLUMN — a tick, a radio and Woo’s own checkbox, one text rail

page rail control rail text rail

Three components, three files, two rails — one for the control and one for the text, and all three families on both. They were 1.18em, 1.15rem and 1.25rem: three sizes for one job, so a form that mixed them put its text on rails up to 3.5 px apart. Too small to name, exactly large enough to make a form feel loose. One token, --control, at the size the owner had already approved, and the em one is gone — an em control changed size with whatever font-size its label happened to have.

The control is inset from the row’s edge by the same gap it keeps on its other side. Sitting exactly on the rail it had --inline of air to its right, before the label, and none at all to its left. The row’s own box still starts on the rail — this is padding inside it, not a margin on it — so a list of tickboxes still lines up with the headings and fields above it.

The heading sits closer to what it names than blocks sit to each other — --stack-tight after a heading, --stack between blocks — so a title reads as belonging to the thing under it rather than floating between two. The gap is between: the first block starts flush against the top of its column and the last one leaves no trailing hole, which a margin on the block itself cannot do.

What this section is for. B1 of the checkout port is “the form’s own frame”, and the honest way to do it is not to write rules for the checkout — it is to have a frame, a split and a rhythm that every page uses, and then let the checkout be one of them. Anything still declaring its own max-width:var(--page-max) is on the list: .d-grid, .d-archive, .d-product, .d-hero, .d-404 and .d-section-title all predate .d-shell and still agree with it by hand.

Rules

Composition — every primitive inside every other, and the awkward real ones

“How do we know that if we put a checkbox next to a table, inside a panel, inside a table, it will display properly?” You do not, and neither does anyone else, because reasoning does not survive two levels of nesting. You render it and you measure it. That is this section, and scripts/matrixgate.js is the measuring.

Every cell below is two of the inner primitive inside one of the outer one, with the same two boxes at the bottom of all of them. Two, because a stack with one child and a cluster with one child are the same thing — nothing — and the first version of this grid had exactly that, so twenty of the twenty-five cells were showing the inner primitive and saying nothing about the outer. The cells are outlined, so a child escaping its container is visible as well as measurable.

What each one is. .d-stack is a column: things one under another, one gap between each. .d-cluster is a row that wraps: things side by side at their natural widths, wrapping individually when they run out of room. .d-switcher is a row that becomes a column all at once: equal widths, and either all beside each other or all stacked, decided by how wide its container is and never half and half. .d-box is not a layout at all — it is a surface with padding, and the only thing allowed to inset its contents. .d-split is a main column with a fixed-width companion beside it that drops underneath when there is no room.

The gate asserts three things over the whole section: nothing sticks out past its container, no padded box sits alone inside another padded box, and every component rendered on its own has zero outer margin.

4 · a field inside a box inside a table cell, beside WooCommerce’s own field

EVERY COMPONENT ON ITS OWN — the gate reads the outer margin off each of these

A component must not set its own outer margin: the gap between two things belongs to whatever contains them, because only the container knows what the two things are. Each dashed box below holds one component as an only child, so a margin has nowhere to hide.

What this section cannot do. It proves the combinations it contains and nothing else, and it is a fixed list — the five primitives crossed with themselves plus four real arrangements. It will not find a bug in a nesting nobody wrote down. That is a real limit and the answer to it is to add rows when a new arrangement appears on the site, which is cheap because the grid is generated.

And one primitive is missing from the grid on purpose. .d-grid still carries the page frame — max-width, centring and --gutter — because its markup is WordPress block templates where a class is written twice. Nested in a 230 px cell that is 60 px of gutter each side and nothing left over, so it cannot be composed until the templates are regenerated. That is the rest of B1, and it is now a visible consequence rather than a note.

Status

Where this actually stands

The patterns are done and reviewed. Every section above this one has been through the owner, and every one is written against markup captured from the live site rather than against class names. Anything that has to overrule WooCommerce lives in src/adopted/, outside the cascade layers, because that is the only place it can win.

What is left is WooCommerce’s own furniture — the surfaces we do not author but do have to dress. The catalogue filters (above) were the first of four:

A. Catalogue filters — done, and reviewed. Shell and both modes are real; everything below the shell is a floor rather than a finish, and src/adopted/filters.css says so in capitals. Re-verify against the real DOM the day the catalogue has more than one product in it.

B. The block checkout’s innards. Captured with a browser and a seeded cart, because the served page is 3 KB of scaffolding and the entire form is built by React — 141 distinct wc-block classes that curl cannot see. Steps, address form, totals, payment radios, express payment.

C. The two libraries WooCommerce brings with it. select2, which is 230 rules and is live on /my-account/ today, and PhotoSwipe on the product gallery. Each is a decision before it is a stylesheet: dress it, or replace it with something of ours.

D. Woo’s button variants. is-link and is-style-outline arrive from the block editor on content nobody here wrote, and neither has a home in this system yet.

Then the cutover, which has not moved: point functions.php at the built stylesheet, add add_editor_style() so the block editor gets the same file, delete style.css and assets/darling.css, then take WooCommerce’s own stylesheets off one handle at a time in the order set out in the surface inventory.

And two things carried, so they are not quietly lost. The map picker above is the styled component only — the map itself is a later job, and OpenFreeMap with MapLibre is the current answer (no key, no quota, commercial use explicit, self-hostable, and no SLA, which is the catch). And the office-field plugin still emits an inline #b01f30 that wants to become .d-notice--warning.
